previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of type II diabetes, chronic systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and morbid obesity was admitted for bilateral diabetic foot ulcers and peripheral edema. He underwent debridement of the ulcers in the emergency department and was started on oral antibiotics. During the hospitalization, he was evaluated for a vitreous hemorrhage in the left eye, diagnosed via ophthalmology consult, and prescribed eye drops with close outpatient follow-up. He received one dose of IV furosemide for fluid overload and was counseled on compression and wound care. His diabetes and anticoagulation were managed with home medications. He was discharged home the following day with instructions to continue wound care, complete antibiotics, monitor daily weights, and follow up with podiatry, cardiology, ophthalmology, and primary care.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ was admitted with left foot blistering and erythema, 
consistent with left foot cellulitis, thought to be most likely 
secondary to streptococcus spp given extensive blistering. CT 
ruled-out deeper infection, he was started on vancomycin and 
pip/tazo, transitioned to vancomycin and amp/sulbactam, and 
discharged home on bactrim/augmentin. Wound care recommendations 
were used for dressing the left lower extremity which were 
explained to the patient upon discharge.  

ACTIVE ISSUES
# Cellulitis
LLE cellulitis in setting of DM and PVD, with associated 
superficial bullae. No concern for deeper infection on exam and 
CT imaging. With associated bullae, concern for staph infection, 
but given his uncontrolled diabetes with complications, needed 
to cover for gram negatives. Was afebrile and without systemic 
symptoms throughout his hospitalization. Was started on 
vancomycin and pip/tazo but transitioned to vancomycin and 
amp/sulbactam given lack of risk factors or exam findings to 
suggest the need for pseudomonal coverage. Wound care was 
consulted for recommendations on dressings. Podiatry followed 
the patient, and they performed lancing and drainage of the 
bullae without complications. Wound care recommended ___ to 
assist the patient with home wound care, however he declined 
despite being counseled on the risks. He wished to be discharged 
prior to being transitioned to oral antibiotics, so he was 
discharged with a prescription for 7 days bactrim/augmentin. 
Wound cultures taken after lancing by podiatry showed mixed 
bacterial types. 

# Atrial fibrillation on warfarin
Was slightly subtherapeutic with an INR of 1.8 on admission, he 
was continued on his home dose of 5mg warfarin daily and his INR 
bumped into the therapeutic range. It was recommended that he 
take 4mg warfarin daily while on the course of bactrim.

# Dilated CM with mixed systolic and diastolic HF
Last echo ___ with EF ___. Had LLE edema on admission, 
which per patient is ""moderate"" for him. No other signs or 
symptoms of decompensation. Reports taking a range of torsemide 
at home from ___ daily depending upon the degree of edema, 
altough per ___ cardiology note dated ___ he was increased 
to 100mg daily. He was given 80mg torsemide daily and diuresed 
well. He was continued on ASA, spironolactone, ramipril, 
metoprolol

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  Extensive redness and blistering of left foot and calf.  Evaluate
for necrotizing fasciitis.

COMPARISON:  Radiographs of the bilateral feet dated ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were obtained from the knee to the bottom of the foot
after the administration of 100 cc of Omnipaque intravenous contrast.  Coronal
and sagittal reformats were constructed.

DLP:  752.66 mGy-cm.

FINDINGS:  There is extensive soft tissue swelling and fat stranding at the
base of the foot and at the calf.  No focal rim-enhancing fluid collection is
seen to suggest abscess.  No subcutaneous gas is detected.  No cortical
destruction is seen.  Extensive vascular calcifications are noted throughout
the vessels of the lower extremities.  An os trigonum is noted posterior to
the talus.  No fracture or dislocation is identified.  The joint spaces of the
foot are relatively well maintained.  No joint effusion of the ankle is seen.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No CT evidence of abscess, necrotizing fasciitis, or osteomyelitis.
2.  Soft tissue swelling and fat stranding which can be consistent with
cellulitis.
3.  Extensive vascular calcifications.
